title: Admission + Fallback probe: latency & cost notes
body:
Purpose:
Quick internal benchmark sketch to compare simple probabilistic admission control vs cheap-model fallback vs combined policy under short microburst spikes. Goal: show practical latency / cost tradeoffs and surface operational caveats for rollout. Not exhaustive -- rough lab notes, experiments run on testbed cluster (see linked artifacts).

Testbed summary:
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB (core pool), 2x T4 (cheap-fallback pool).
- Runtime: Redwood runtime nightly (commit 7f3b2), dynamic batching enabled, KV cache off for these runs to isolate admission/fallback effects.
- Models:
  * model-big: open-llama-65b-8k (A100) -- baseline production variant.
  * model-small: vicuna-7b-q4 (T4) -- fallback cheap model.
- Traffic: synthetic client replay of 10k sessions with microbursts: baseline sustained 50 qps for 5m, then 30s spike to 800 qps repeated 6x. Payloads: mixed length (prompt median 60 tokens, tail 600 tokens).
- Cost assumptions: A100 per-second cost = $0.75 (amortized infra), T4 per-second = $0.08. Tokenized cost normalized to per-1k output tokens using measured throughput. These are rough for comparative purpose only.

Policies tested (short names used below):
- BASELINE: no admission, all requests to model-big; queueing + batching normal.
- ADMIT-PROB(0.5): probabilistic admission gate during spike windows which drops 50% of new requests (reject with 429-equivalent), remaining 50% proceed to model-big. No fallback.
- FALLBACK: admission gate disabled; when queue length > threshold, route new requests to model-small instead of model-big (best-effort).
- HYBRID: probabilistic admission (30%) + fallback for remainder when queue>threshold.

Metrics captured (per-run): p50/p90/p99 latency (server-side), observed throughput (requests/s served), effective success rate (no-reject), estimated infra cost per 1k output tokens, qualitative quality delta (manual sample inspect).

Key numeric snapshot (aggregated across 6 spikes, averaged):
- BASELINE:
  p50: 85 ms | p90: 310 ms | p99: 1,420 ms
  throughput served: 100% of requests (no rejects)
  cost per 1k tokens: $2.45
  quality: baseline model-big quality 

- ADMIT-PROB(0.5):
  p50: 60 ms | p90: 170 ms | p99: 650 ms
  throughput served: 50% (others rejected)
  cost per 1k tokens (served): $1.40 (note: user-perceived cost depends on billing/retry policy)
  quality: same as baseline for served subset (rejected requests show degraded UX)

- FALLBACK:
  p50: 95 ms | p90: 240 ms | p99: 830 ms
  throughput served: ~98% (few queue-timeouts)
  cost per 1k tokens: $1.05 (largely due to routing to T4 for many tokens)
  quality: noticeable quality regression on complex prompts (~12% of samples flagged as "low coherence" in inspection)

- HYBRID (admit 30% + fallback):
  p50: 55 ms | p90: 145 ms | p99: 520 ms
  throughput served: ~70% (30% intentionally rejected)
  cost per 1k tokens: $0.95 (best observed for combined UX/cost metric)
  quality: good for admitted subset; fallback quality acceptable for short-turn interactions, problematic for long-context summarization tasks.

Quick ascii chart: p90 latency (ms) by policy (lower is better)
BASELINE  |████████████████████████████████████| 310
ADMIT-50% |███████████████                    | 170
FALLBACK   |█████████████████████             | 240
HYBRID     |██████████████                     | 145

Throughput served (%): BASELINE 100% | ADMIT-50% 50% | FALLBACK 98% | HYBRID 70%
Cost per 1k tokens (USD): BASELINE $2.45 | ADMIT-50% $1.40 | FALLBACK $1.05 | HYBRID $0.95

Observations / interpretation:
- Admission-only reduces tail latency significantly (p99 cut ~55%), but UX hit from rejections is severe if clients don't retry intelligently. For front-door APIs, this may be acceptable for low-priority routes.
- Fallback lowers cost materially and preserves served-rate, but quality regressions are non-trivial for long-context and multi-step tasks; meter which request types are safe for fallback (e.g., short Q&A vs summarization).
- Hybrid policy yields the best compromise: keep a deterministic fraction of high-quality responses, spill low-priority traffic to fallback, and reject the remaining fraction. This pattern lowered $/token and p99 simultaneously in our synthetic spikes.
- KV cache disabled here; adding an effective cache would amplify benefits of fallback (more short-turns can be served cheaply) and make admission less necessary. Need follow-up runs with KV hit-rate sweep.

Operational caveats found during runs:
- Sudden switch to fallback causes transient model load flapping if routing decisions are synchronous; add hysteresis (2s hold window) to prevent oscillation.
- Metric attribution: cost-per-1k tokens can look artificially low for FALLBACK because smaller model produces shorter outputs (compression bias). Need normalization by gold-output-length for fair quality-adjusted cost.
- Client retry behaviour changes effective served-rate; we observed backoff from our synthetic client reduced observed rejects vs naive retry. Product should define retry semantics for admission.

Small sample quality notes (manual):
- FALLBACK errors concentrated on long-context composition, hallucination rate + confidence mismatch in model-small.
- For quick factual Qs (<40 tokens) model-small was acceptable in ~92% cases.

Recommended next steps:
1) Add KV cache ON runs with 20/50/80% hit-rate to measure interaction with fallback.
2) Sweep admission probabilities (10/30/50/70) and queue thresholds; produce iso-cost latency curves.
3) Run mixed workload with real prod traces (sanitized) to validate sample distribution effects.
4) Prototype hybrid rollout: start with low-risk endpoints (embeddings, short Q&A) and measure customer impact.
5) Add telemetry flags: "served-model", "admission-reason", "fallback-reason" to link to SLO budgeting and billing.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to represent partial credit in billing when fallback returns lower-quality output? (billing/CS question)
- Should we expose soft-admission (queue position header) to clients so they can choose to upgrade to paid fast path?
- Need standard quality rubric and automated evaluation to quantify "acceptable" fallback for each product route.

Notes to self: link to experiments in repo, attach raw traces (trace ids in linked_artifacts). This doc is a sketch for product + runtime to discuss rollout strategy. Keep as draft until follow-up runs (KV on + real trace) complete.

-- Samira
